PAPER: RESEARCH ARTICLE Published Online: October 4, 2025 https://doi.org/10.31893/multiscience.2026276 Can Islamic branding and religiosity enhance the financial performance of halal MSMEs? An explanatory study Sulton Sholehuddinab | Agung Winarnoa | Heri Pratiktoa | Imam Mukhlisa | Budi Eko Soetjiptoa aFaculty of Economics and Business, Universitas Negeri Malang, Malang, Indonesia. bFaculty of Economics and Business, Universitas Islam Malang, Malang, Indonesia. Abstract The purpose of this study is to assess how the financial performance of halal MSMEs is impacted by Islamic branding, religiosity, Islamic financial literacy, and an entrepreneurial mindset. Using quantitative methods and an explanatory research approach, this study the causal links among these variables. Islamic branding and Islamic financial literacy were found to have a significant and positive influence on the financial performance of halal MSMEs, whereas the moderating effects of entrepreneurship orientation and religiosity were not significant. Data collection was conducted via a validated and reliable questionnaire that targeted a sample of 224 halal MSMEs located in Malang city and Regency. The analysis, performed through the SEM‒PLS technique, revealed that Islamic branding and Islamic financial literacy are crucial factors in enhancing the financial performance of halal MSMEs, whereas other variables exhibited a lesser or negligible impact. Furthermore, Islamic financial literacy serves as a mediator in the link between Islamic branding and financial performance, whereas entrepreneurship orientation does not significantly influence the link between religiosity and financial performance. The inference of this research makes a valuable contribution to the existing body of literature and offers practical recommendations for halal MSME entrepreneurs to increase their business performance by adopting effective branding strategies, managing finances in accordance with various principles, and fostering an entrepreneurial orientation. Additionally, this research aims to aid policymakers in developing supportive policies for the growth of halal MSMEs in Indonesia. The limitations of this study include the small sample size and the use of survey methods; thus, further research with more comprehensive methods and variables is needed. Keywords: Islamic branding, religiosity, financial performance, Islamic financial literacy, entrepreneurship orientation 1. Introduction In many nations, including Indonesia, micro, small-, and medium-sized enterprises (MSMEs) form the foundation of the economy. MSMEs are crucial for boosting economic growth, lowering poverty, and generating jobs (Irawan & Sukiyono, 2021). Considering that Muslims make up the majority of Indonesia's population, halal MSMEs have emerged as one of the industries that has received much attention as time has changed. Halal MSMEs prioritize business practices that align with Islamic principles in addition to the halal nature of their goods (Puspitaningrum et al., 2021). Two ideas that are becoming increasingly important in the context of halal MSMEs are Islamic branding and religiosity. Islamic branding can be defined as a marketing strategy that uses Islamic values and symbols to attract Muslim consumers (Widyakto et al., 2024; Winarno & Nadia, 2021). In the context of halting MSMEs, Islamic branding can help increase consumer awareness, strengthen customer loyalty, and ultimately improve financial performance. A good reputation and strong identity through Islamic Branding can provide a competitive advantage for halal MSMEs (Mardikaningsih et al., 2024). On the other hand, religiosity reflects the extent to which religious beliefs and practices influence a person's life and decisions. For Muslim entrepreneurs, religiosity can influence financial decision-making and overall business management. Religious company owners typically operate their companies in accordance with sharia law, which can improve financial results (Alshehri et al., 2021; Mukhlis et al., 2022). However, Islamic financial literacy and entrepreneurship orientation also need to be considered in this context. Understanding sharia-compliant financial principles is known as Islamic financial literacy. Halal MSME owners can reduce financial risk and manage their money more skillfully and efficiently with a solid grasp of Islamic financial literacy (Saifurrahman & Kassim, 2021). Entrepreneurship orientation includes attitudes, values, and behaviors that encourage innovation, proactivity, and risk taking in business. Halal MSME entrepreneurs who have a strong entrepreneurship orientation tend to be more innovative and responsive to market changes, which can ultimately improve financial performance (Deku et al., 2023; Pratikto et al., 2023; Rauf et al., 2022). Entrepreneurs who have high entrepreneurship orientation tend to be more adaptive to market changes and more innovative in developing products and services (Zighan et al., 2022; Priyanto et al., 2022). A strong identity and good reputation through Islamic branding can provide a significant competitive advantage for halting MSMEs (Islam, 2021). For Muslim entrepreneurs, religiosity can influence financial decision-making and overall business management. Religious entrepreneurs tend to run their businesses in accordance with sharia principles, which can have a positive effect on financial performance (Elhoushy & Jang, 2021). First, how does Islamic branding affect the financial performance of halal MSMEs? Second, what impact does religiosity have on halal MSMEs' financial performance and financial decision-making? Third, how does the link between Islamic branding and the financial performance of halal MSMEs be mediated by Islamic financial literacy? Fourth, how is the link between religiosity and the financial success of halal MSMEs tempered by entrepreneurial orientation? Fifth, how do Islamic financial literacy and entrepreneurship orientation together affect the financial performance of halal MSMEs? The main objective of this study is to evaluate the role of Islamic branding, religiosity, Islamic financial literacy, and entrepreneurship orientation in increasing the financial performance of halal MSMEs. Literature Review The comprehension of and familiarity with financial concepts that align with Sharia law is known as Islamic financial literacy. These guidelines include preventing riba (interest), promoting honest and open business dealings, and controlling risk in a way that aligns with Islamic beliefs. Knowledge of halal financial services and products, including Islamic banking, Islamic insurance (takaful), and Islamic investing, is necessary to comprehend Islamic financial literacy (Widarni & Bawono, 2021). Managing the money of halal MSMEs requires a high level of Islamic financial literacy. Entrepreneurs may make more prudent financial decisions that align with Islamic ideals by having a solid grasp of the fundamentals of Islamic finance (Majid & Nugraha, 2022). Compliance with Sharia principles ensures that halal MSME entrepreneurs run their businesses in accordance with religious law, which increases business credibility and attracts consumers who prioritize halal products and services. In addition, understanding Islamic financial literacy helps entrepreneurs manage financial risk more effectively (Raimi et al., 2025). The prohibition of usury encourages the use of fairer and more transparent financing methods, optimizes financial management by choosing financing options that best suit business needs, and encourages innovation in the development of halal products and services, which in turn helps halal MSMEs achieve sustainable growth and increase competitiveness in the market (Siregar et al., 2023). Islamic Branding is a marketing strategy that uses Islamic values and symbols to attract Muslim consumers. Islamic Branding not only includes the use of an Islamic name or logo but also entails applying Islamic values to every facet of the company, including products, services, and communication with consumers (Ansori et al., 2023). The influence of Islamic branding on financial performance can be seen from several aspects. First, Islamic Branding can increase customer loyalty by building a strong relationship between consumers and brands. Muslim customers are more likely to stick with companies that share their values and beliefs, which reduces churn rates and increases customer retention. Second, Islamic branding helps halal MSMEs to expand their market by attracting Muslim consumers worldwide. In the era of globalization, Muslim consumers have greater access to halal products and services, so brands with strong Islamic Branding can reach a wider market share. Third, with increasing consumer awareness of halal products, Islamic Branding can increase sales by attracting consumers who are more aware of the importance of sharia-compliant products. Products with halal certification and clear Islamic branding tend to sell better on the market (Ab Hamid et al., 2023). Consumer awareness is also influenced by Islamic branding. Islamic Branding helps develop a positive perception of the brand in the minds of Muslim customers. The use of Islamic symbols in branding increases consumer trust in the products and services offered. Marketing campaigns that evoke Islamic values can attract consumers' attention and differentiate products from competitors. In addition, Islamic Branding helps strengthen brand identity by reflecting Islamic values and principles, which builds a more emotional connection with consumers, increasing consumer loyalty and trust (Salehzadeh et al., 2023). Religiosity is the degree to which a person lives and practices religious teachings in their daily lives. From the perspective of Islamic financial concepts, its operational activities are without an interest system and use a profit-sharing mechanism, individuals with strong religious beliefs are more likely to support the Islamic financial system (Novianto et al, 2025). For Muslim entrepreneurs, religiosity can influence financial decision-making and overall business management. Religious Muslim entrepreneurs tend to adhere more to sharia principles when running their businesses. This includes avoiding usury practices, conducting fair transactions, and managing risks in accordance with Islamic teachings. Compliance with sharia principles increases business credibility and attracts consumers who prioritize halal products. Religiosity also encourages entrepreneurs to run businesses with higher ethics, including transparency in transactions, honesty in business, and fairness in resource management (Sholihin et al., 2022). This high level of business ethics enhances business reputation and builds consumer trust. In addition, religious Muslim entrepreneurs tend to make wiser financial decisions, considering the long-term impact of each decision, which helps them manage finances more effectively and avoid unnecessary risks. Religiosity also encourages entrepreneurs to engage in social and charitable activities, which enhances business image and attracts consumers who care about social issues, as well as having a positive effect on financial performance by increasing customer loyalty and creating stronger relationships with the community (Fatmawati & Fauzan, 2021; Triatmanto et al., 2023). Entrepreneurship orientation is an attitude, value, and https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Sholehuddin et al. (2026) 4 behavior that drives innovation, proactivity, and risk taking in business. Halal MSME entrepreneurs who have a strong entrepreneurship orientation tend to be more innovative and responsive to market changes. Entrepreneurs are encouraged by an entrepreneurship orientation to create new goods and services that address unmet customer demands. This innovation helps halal MSMEs to increase their competitiveness and attract new consumers (Corrêa et al., 2022). Entrepreneurs with high entrepreneurship orientation tend to be more proactive in facing market changes and quickly respond to new trends and business opportunities, which helps halal MSMEs to remain competitive in an ever-evolving market. Entrepreneurship orientation encourages entrepreneurs to take calculated risks in pursuing business opportunities, and entrepreneurs who dare to take risks tend to be more successful in creating innovation and growing their businesses. Strong entrepreneurship orientation can help halal MSMEs achieve better business performance. Entrepreneurs who are innovative, proactive, and dare to take risks tend to be more successful in achieving sustainable growth and increasing the profitability of their businesses (Rassool et al., 2023). Strong Islamic Branding is expected to increase consumer awareness, customer loyalty, and ultimately the financial performance of halal MSMEs. Halal MSMEs that use Islamic symbols in their branding and actively communicate their commitment to sharia principles are more attractive to Muslim consumers, which in turn improves their financial performance. Religious Muslim entrepreneurs tend to adhere more to sharia principles in running their businesses, which can improve financial performance through high business ethics and wise financial decisions. Religious entrepreneurs focus more on fairness in transactions and transparency in financial management, which increases consumer trust and customer loyalty. Consumer awareness of the value of sharia financial goods and Islamic financial literacy may be increased by effective Islamic branding (Mardikaningsih et al., 2024). The financial performance of halal MSMEs may be enhanced by strong Islamic branding, which can also increase Islamic financial knowledge. Marketing initiatives that promote Islamic principles, for example, can increase customer awareness of the benefits of Islamic financial literacy, which in turn enhances the financial performance of halal MSMEs. Entrepreneurs' religiosity can increase Islamic financial literacy, which ultimately improves the financial performance of halal MSMEs (Supriadi et al., 2023). High-entrepreneurship orientation can strengthen the influence of Islamic financial literacy on the financial performance of MSMEs by encouraging innovation and wise risk taking. Sharia Enterprise theory (SET) integrates sharia values into the theory of the company. This theory emphasizes that the purpose of a company is not only to seek economic profit but also to consider social and spiritual aspects. Shariah Enterprise Theory (SET) encourages company owners to operate their companies in line with sharia values, including social responsibility, justice, and transparency, in the context of halal MSMEs (Raimi et al., 2025). Signaling theory explains how information conveyed by companies can influence the investment decisions of consumers and investors. In the context of Islamic Branding, companies that convey information about sharia compliance and Islamic values in their businesses can provide positive signals to Muslim consumers. This can increase consumer trust and encourage purchasing decisions (Zulkarnain et al., 2024). Islamic financial literacy is another area where signaling theory is essential. Businesses can draw in more clients and investors by offering clear and understandable information regarding various financial goods and services. Accurate and reliable information helps consumers and investors make wiser decisions, which can ultimately improve a company's financial performance (Susbiyani et al., 2023). Knowledge is a company's primary resource that may provide it with a competitive edge, according to the knowledge- based view (KBV). Understanding the fundamentals of Islamic branding, Islamic finance, and entrepreneurship is crucial for halting MSMEs to attain the best possible financial results (Cuthbertson & Furseth, 2022). Entrepreneurs may establish competitive advantages that are difficult for rivals to copy by combining their understanding of Islamic branding with Islamic financial literacy (Hasan et al., 2024; Ullah et al., 2023). To assess the impacts of Islamic branding, religiosity, Islamic financial literacy, and entrepreneurship orientation on the financial performance of halal MSMEs, this study proposes several hypotheses that are evaluated in light of the theoretical framework that has been established. H1: Financial performance is significantly improved by Islamic branding. H2: Financial success is significantly improved by religiosity. H3: Islamic financial literacy is significantly improved by Islamic branding. H4: Islamic financial literacy is significantly enhanced by religiosity. H5: Financial performance is significantly improved by Islamic financial literacy. H6: The relationship between Islamic branding and financial success is mediated by Islamic financial literacy. H7: The relationship between religiosity and financial success is mediated by Islamic financial literacy. H8: Financial performance is significantly improved by an entrepreneurial mindset. H9: The association between Islamic financial literacy and financial performance is strengthened by an entrepreneurial orientation. It is anticipated that by putting these theories into the test, this study will shed lighter on the variables affecting the financial performance of halal MSMEs and how business owners can maximize their plans via sharia law, Islamic branding, religiosity, Islamic financial literacy, and an entrepreneurial mindset. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Sholehuddin et al. (2026) 5 3. Materials and Methods This study combines an explanatory research strategy with a quantitative research methodology. Because it can provide an objective picture of the relationships among the variables under study, a quantitative technique was used. By taking into account the roles of the mediator (Islamic financial literacy) and moderator (entrepreneurship orientation), the explanatory research approach seeks to explain the link of causality between the independent variables (Islamic branding and religiosity) and the dependent variable (financial performance of halal MSMEs). For the Islamic Branding variable, the indicators used include compliance, origin, and customers. For the Religiosity variable, the indicators measured are ideological, ritualistic, intellectual, consequential, and experiential. Moreover, indicators of Islamic financial knowledge, Islamic financial awareness, and Islamic financial attitudes are used to measure the Islamic financial literacy variable. The entrepreneurship orientation variable is measured on the basis of proactive, risk taking, and competitive aggressiveness. The financial performance of halal MSMEs is measured through indicators of productivity, sales growth, and profitability. This quantitative approach uses a questionnaire instrument created especially for this study to collect structured data. Before being utilized in the study, this questionnaire's questions were examined for validity and reliability and were pertinent to the research issue. Table 1 presents an operational description of the variables. The study focused on culinary SMEs with halal certification located in Malang City and Malang Regency, Indonesia comprising a total population of 535 enterprises (240 in Malang City and 295 in Malang Regency). Sampling was carried out using a purposive technique, with the inclusion criteria limited to owners or managers of halal-certified SMEs who maintained organized financial records. The sample size was determined using the Raosoft calculator with a 5% margin of error and 50% response distribution, resulting in a required sample of 224 respondents. This procedure was adopted to ensure that the data collected were representative of the population and suitable for generalization. To ensure the research ethics in this study, we explained our research to the respondents, as well as their rights to withdraw from the study at any time. In addition, we also asked their consents to participate voluntarily in this study. The respondents’ profiles were also kept confidential and made anonymous in this study. Data were collected using a purpose-designed questionnaire developed to measure Islamic branding, religiosity, Islamic financial literacy, entrepreneurial orientation, and financial performance of halal culinary SMEs. Each construct was operationalized through multiple statements rated on a five-point Likert scale ranging from 1 = “Strongly Disagree” to 5 = “Strongly Agree.” The instrument was reviewed by leaders of the halal-certified culinary cooperative and the SMEs association to ensure clarity and contextual relevance. Enumerators, under the supervision of association leaders, distributed 250 questionnaires to eligible SME owners and managers and verified the completeness of responses. Returned questionnaires were screened, and incomplete or invalid entries (26 responses) were excluded prior to analysis to maintain data quality. All participants confirmed their voluntary participation in the study and were informed that their responses would be treated with confidentiality. 4. Results 4.1. Discussion This study offers comprehensive insights into how the financial performance of halal MSMEs is impacted by Islamic branding, religion, Islamic financial literacy, and an entrepreneurial mindset. The findings indicate that while religion and entrepreneurship orientation do not significantly affect the financial performance of halal MSMEs, Islamic branding and Islamic financial literacy do. These findings have important theoretical and practical implications that can provide valuable guidance for halal MSME entrepreneurs in developing their business strategies. Islamic branding is proven to have a significant and positive influence on the financial performance of halal MSMEs. This finding shows that branding based on Islamic values can increase consumer perceptions of quality, trust, and loyalty. According to branding theory, strong brand attributes can create a positive brand image and customer loyalty, as found by Ab Hamid et al. (2023). Islamic branding not only increases business visibility and reputation but also strengthens emotional connections with consumers who value Islamic values. Implementing a branding strategy that adheres to sharia principles may provide MSMEs with a major competitive edge in the marketplace. However, the findings of this study demonstrated that religion had no discernible effect on the financial performance of halal MSMEs. This result differs from other research findings that religiosity can increase financial efficiency and decrease waste (Elhoushy & Jang, 2021). However, Alshehri et al. (2021) revealed that religion had a stronger effect on adherence to sustainable and ethical business practices. Although religious beliefs may not be explicitly represented in financial success in the context of halal MSMEs, they can reinforce a dedication to sharia-compliant business operations. Religious values can play a role in building a good reputation and increasing consumer trust, although their impact may not be immediately visible in financial performance. Islamic financial literacy was also found to have a significant and positive effect on the financial performance of halal MSMEs. Good financial literacy helps entrepreneurs make wiser and more efficient financial decisions, as supported by Hasan et al. (2024). Furthermore, the link between Islamic branding and financial success is mediated by Islamic financial knowledge. This demonstrates how successful branding tactics and better financial performance may result from a thorough grasp of Islamic financial concepts such as usury, zakat, and profit sharing. Additionally, this study revealed that Islamic financial literacy is significantly impacted by Islamic branding, indicating that branding can shape consumer behavior and understanding of finance, as explained by Majid and Nugraha (2022). Nonetheless, the results suggest that the financial success of halal MSMEs is not significantly impacted by the entrepreneurial approach. This may be due to other factors, such as limited resources or a less supportive business https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Sholehuddin et al. (2026) 8 environment. Although the theory states that entrepreneurial orientation can improve business performance through innovation and risk taking, as explained by Corrêa et al. (2022), the results of this study indicate that in the context of halal MSMEs, other factors may play a greater role. Limited resources, a less supportive business environment, or a lack of access to a wider market may hinder the effect of entrepreneurial orientation on financial performance. Halal MSME entrepreneurs greatly benefit from the practical consequences of this study. First, entrepreneurs should focus on developing branding strategies that reflect Islamic values to increase consumer trust and loyalty. Effective communication of Islamic values should be an integral part of the marketing strategy. Using Islamic symbols, such as Arabic calligraphy or halal logos, can increase brand visibility and attract consumers who value sharia principles. Second, education and training on Islamic financial concepts such as usury, zakat, and profit sharing are essential to help MSME entrepreneurs make better financial decisions. Financial literacy programs that involve practical training and real case studies can improve understanding and financial management skills. With a good understanding of Islamic finance, entrepreneurs can plan and manage their finances more wisely, avoid practices that are contrary to sharia principles, and maximize profit potential. The next finding shows a robust link between IFL and financial performance, confirming some prior studies (e.g., Putri et al., 2024; Suseno et al., 2021). The underlying reason of this study notes that beyond religious values, the capacity of entrepreneurs to understand financial knowledge rooted in Islamic principles plays a central role in dealing with business outcomes. In the context of sharia, careful financial planning is considered part of achieving sustainable blessings and success (Rahadjeng et al., 2023). In addition, this attitude reflects the integration of Islamic values in business management, where customers not only focus on material benefits but also moral and social responsibility in the management of funds (Alshebami & Murad, 2022). Third, although religiosity does not directly affect financial performance, religious values can be used to strengthen commitment to ethical and sustainable business practices. Halal MSME entrepreneurs must prioritize ethical principles in every aspect of their business, from production to service to consumers. By implementing ethical principles, entrepreneurs can build a good reputation, increase consumer trust, and create long-term mutually beneficial relationships. A prior work noted that entrepreneurs with religiosity are perceived by consumers as more trustworthy, which can drive customer retention (Dinh et al., 2022). In this way, religiosity can indirectly contribute to financial performance by aligning businesses with the expectations of halal markets. However, the results of this study indicate that religiosity does not significantly influence IFL, which is contrary to prior studies (e.g., Alharbi et al., 2022; Desiyanti & Kassim, 2020). This asymmetry suggests that while values and beliefs can guide ethical and strategic choices. In this case, the results be explained that the necessary translation into technical competence in managing financial matters, such as budgeting, credit, and risk management. Fourth, although the results of this study indicate that entrepreneurial orientation is not significant, halal MSME entrepreneurs must still encourage innovation and healthy risk-taking in running their businesses. Product innovation, service quality improvement, and new market development can help improve competitiveness and financial performance. Entrepreneurs should also seek opportunities to collaborate with Islamic financial institutions, the government, and nongovernmental organizations to gain the necessary support in developing their businesses. By emphasizing the value of Islamic branding and Islamic financial literacy in enhancing the financial performance of halal MSMEs, this study significantly adds to the body of current material. The results also offer halal MSME owner helpful pointers for creating successful business plans grounded in sharia law. However, this study has several limitations, including a small sample size and restricted geographic emphasis, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. Therefore, to improve the generalizability of the findings, further research with larger and more varied populations is needed. To obtain a more thorough grasp of the elements influencing the financial success of halal MSMEs, future studies should also consider other variables, including product innovation, service quality, and customer happiness. This finding contrasts with much of the established literature (e.g., Wales et al., 2021; Covin & Wales, 2019), which positions EO as a driver of firm performance. One possible explanation lies in the contextual realities faced by halal SMEs. Many operate in resource-constrained environments where entrepreneurial efforts do not directly translate into measurable financial outcomes (Jewer et al., 2024). For instance, being innovative and proactive can create new products or services, but without sufficient digital infrastructure, they fail to reach profitability (Paul Jr et al., 2024). Similarly, risk-taking behaviors can lead SMEs to vulnerabilities in uncertain markets, primarily when compliance with Islamic principles limits the range of financing and investment options available (Ureta, 2021). Furthermore, the mediation analysis indicates that IFL can mediate Islamic branding and financial performance, with a partial mediation status. In essence, Islamic branding fosters performance both on its own and by elevating the financial competencies of SME owners. This finding aligns with prior research conducted in Indonesia, where IFL was provided as a significant mediator between Islamic branding and SMEs’ performance (Hanifah et al., 2024). Another important result from this study is the full mediation role of IFL in the relationship between religiosity and financial performance. The basic rationale to support this result is that religiosity provides the ethical orientation and motivation for entrepreneurs, but without IFL, these values cannot be effectively operationalized in resource management, investment, or risk control. This outcome is consistent with recent empirical work. Putri et al. (2024) found that religiosity significantly influences Islamic financial literacy and the performance of SMEs. https://www.malque.pub/ojs/index.php/msj Sholehuddin et al. (2026) 9 The moderation analysis indicates that EO does not significantly moderate the relationship between Islamic branding and financial performance, as well as between religiosity and financial performance of SMEs in Indonesia, with both interaction terms proving insignificant. This result contrasts with previous studies that highlight EO as a main driver that can promote the effect of external and internal resources on performance, primarily through innovativeness and risk-taking behavior (Mathafena & Msimango-Galawe, 2023; Covin & Wales, 2019). Concerning halal SMEs, however, the findings suggest that branding and religiosity exert direct and dominant influences on financial performance, diminishing the potential role of EO. Capturing from the perspective of the Resource-Based View (Barney, 1991), EO is expected to act as a capability that transforms resources into superior outcomes. However, in this case, the moderating role is absent, possibly due to constraints in managerial resources or digital adoption. In addition, the possible explanation to support this finding is due to the lack of organizational routines necessary to translate orientation into performance leverage. These findings, therefore, highlight that while EO is important, its benefits for halal SMEs do not materialize without adequate institutional support or digital infrastructure that promotes orientation to interact with other performance drivers. Future studies can improve our knowledge of the elements affecting the financial performance of halal MSMEs and offer more precise and useful advice while keeping these limits in mind. Further research can also use mixed methods, including in-depth interviews and case studies, to reduce respondent bias and gain deeper insights. Thus, this study not only provides theoretical contributions but also provides valuable practical implications for halal MSME entrepreneurs in improving their business performance in accordance with sharia principles. 6. Conclusions In the context of halal MSMEs, this research demonstrates that Islamic branding and Islamic financial literacy significantly and favorably impact financial performance. The importance of establishing branding on the basis of Islamic principles is demonstrated by the fact that Islamic branding has emerged as the most significant element that positively affects financial performance. Furthermore, improved financial success is correlated with a high level of Islamic financial knowledge. Nonetheless, there is no discernible moderating influence of religiosity or entrepreneurial orientation on financial performance. By emphasizing the importance of Islamic elements in enhancing the financial performance of halal MSMEs, this study adds to the body of previous knowledge. On the basis of the findings of this study, some practical suggestions for halting the financial performance of MSMEs include strengthening Islamic Branding with a focus on developing branding strategies that reflect Islamic values, including the display of products in line with Islamic beliefs and the successful dissemination of these ideals to customers. In addition, halal MSME owners and managers should improve their knowledge and understanding of Islamic finance through training and education related to Islamic financial concepts, which can help in making better financial decisions. Although religiosity does not directly affect financial performance, religious values can be used to strengthen commitment to ethical and sustainable business practices, which can ultimately improve consumer reputation and trust. Many limitations should be considered in this study, including the small sample size and the specific geographic region, which may limit the generalizability of the findings. To increase the generalizability of the results, future research should employ larger and more diverse sample sizes. In addition, only a few exogenous constructs were considered in this model, so future research should include additional variables such as product innovation, service quality, and client satisfaction to obtain a more thorough comprehension. The data collection method, which uses a survey that may be susceptible to respondent bias, is also a limitation of this study. Further research can use mixed methods, including in-depth interviews and case studies, to reduce bias and gain deeper insights. Future studies can improve our knowledge of the elements affecting the financial performance of halal MSMEs and offer more precise and useful advice by taking these limitations into account. JSON: Name: islamic_branding_ifl_finperf Title: PLS-SEM analysis of the effects of Islamic branding, religiosity, Islamic financial literacy, and entrepreneurial orientation on the financial performance of halal MSMEs Short Hypothesis: Enhancing Islamic branding practices increases the financial performance of halal MSMEs, and this positive effect is mediated by higher Islamic financial literacy among entrepreneurs. Related Work: Existing empirical work examines individual drivers of halal MSME performance—Islamic branding, religiosity, financial literacy, and entrepreneurial orientation—using cross-sectional surveys and correlational analyses. Common analytical choices include multiple regression and structural equation modeling (both covariance-based SEM and PLS-SEM) to estimate direct effects; fewer studies explicitly test mediation or moderation simultaneously. Limitations across prior approaches include narrow geographical samples, reliance on self-reported single-source data, inconsistent measurement quality for key constructs, underpowered tests for interaction effects, and mixed findings about religiosity and entrepreneurial orientation due to omitted mediators or endogeneity. Prior work rarely compares estimation methods (PLS-SEM vs CB-SEM vs OLS) for robustness, seldom conducts comprehensive measurement-model validation (convergent and discriminant validity, reliability), and seldom reports effect-size metrics or bootstrap-based inference for indirect effects. As a result, causal pathways and the relative contribution of branding versus financial literacy remain unresolved and sensitive to model specification. Abstract: This research investigates whether Islamic branding improves financial performance of halal micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs) and whether Islamic financial literacy mediates that relationship. We propose a quantitative causal model estimated with partial least squares structural equation modeling (PLS-SEM) to quantify direct, indirect, and interaction effects among Islamic branding, religiosity, Islamic financial literacy, entrepreneurial orientation, and firm financial outcomes. The primary contribution is a rigorously validated mediation analysis that isolates the role of Islamic financial literacy as a transmission mechanism from branding to performance while comparing alternative estimators and ablation specifications. Expected outcomes are (1) statistically significant direct effect of Islamic branding on financial performance, (2) a significant indirect effect via Islamic financial literacy, and (3) clarification of the limited moderating role of entrepreneurial orientation and religiosity when tested with adequate power and robust measurement. The results will refine theoretical accounts of resource and signaling pathways in halal MSME performance and inform targeted capacity-building interventions. Experiments: Dataset: primary cross-sectional survey of halal-certified culinary MSMEs expanded beyond Malang to at least three Indonesian regions; target N>=600 to power mediation and moderation tests. Variables: multi-item scales for Islamic branding, religiosity, Islamic financial literacy (IFL), entrepreneurial orientation (EO), and financial performance (productivity, sales growth, profitability); control variables: firm age, firm size, owner education, market segment. Baselines: (A) OLS regressions with aggregated indices; (B) CB-SEM (covariance-based) structural model; (C) PLS-SEM structural model (primary). Estimation: PLS-SEM with reflective measurement models, bootstrap resampling (5,000 samples) for path significance; CB-SEM estimated with maximum likelihood and robust SEs for comparison. Measurement validation: Cronbach's alpha, composite reliability, AVE, HTMT. Evaluation metrics: path coefficients and two-tailed p-values, R^2 per endogenous construct, effect sizes (f2), predictive relevance (Q^2, PLSpredict), model fit indices where applicable (SRMR for PLS, RMSEA/CFI/TLI for CB-SEM), bootstrapped indirect effect magnitude and 95% CI, interaction term significance for moderation. Ablation studies: (1) remove mediator (IFL) to compare direct effect sizes, (2) drop EO interaction terms to test moderation sensitivity, (3) re-estimate with alternative EO operationalizations (e.g., EO sub-dimensions separately). Robustness checks: multi-group analysis by region and firm size, common-method-bias test (Harman's single-factor, marker variable), variance inflation factors for multicollinearity, endogeneity assessment using instrumental variables or Gaussian copula where feasible. Pre-registration: analysis plan pre-registered with primary hypothesis, power analysis, and significance thresholds. Reporting: full path table, indirect-effect decomposition, and comparison of estimator results. Risk Factors and Limitations: Measurement risk: low internal consistency or poor AVE for some constructs (e.g., branding, religiosity) may undermine validity. Common-method bias: single-source self-reported data may inflate associations. Sample/generalization: geographic concentration or sector specificity (culinary halal MSMEs) limits external validity to other industries or countries. Cross-sectional design: temporal ordering and causality remain tentative; reverse causality or simultaneity between branding and performance is possible. Statistical power: moderation tests and multi-group analyses require large samples; underpowered tests may yield false negatives. Model specification: omitted variable bias and misspecified mediation/moderation paths can distort estimates. Estimator limitations: PLS-SEM handles non-normality but provides limited global fit diagnostics; CB-SEM may be sensitive to non-normal data. Endogeneity: unobserved confounders (e.g., unmeasured managerial ability) may bias path coefficients. Response bias: social desirability on religiosity and halal compliance items may distort measures. Scalability: collecting high-quality validated survey data at scale is resource intensive. Computational costs: bootstrap and multi-group procedures increase compute time but are not prohibitive.
